en.summary: A local ice cream shop for a break after walking along Sunset Way. A good way to end the riverside route: try an ice cream with a local flavour, sit down and take in the old railway and neighbourhood streets you just saw.
en.fun_fact: The brand's website records that its second shop opened in Holland Village in 2009, and another opened in the north in 2013. Growing from a neighbourhood shop into a brand across several areas is a local food story in itself.
en.access_notes: Use the address on the official website, 41 Sunset Way. Old pages on visitor platforms still show 14 Sunset Way; this card does not use it.
en.review_summary: 2023 reviews liked being able to taste before choosing and the range of flavours. Some thought it tasted better with a waffle; others didn't like the balance of the lemon pistachio flavour. Some flavours cost extra, so check before ordering.

en.summary: A long-running live seafood restaurant on Sunset Way. Turns an easy neighbourhood walk into a group dinner. Pumpkin sauce crab, seafood bee hoon and orh nee (yam paste) make up a local seafood meal, but ask the weight and market price of live seafood first.
en.fun_fact: The restaurant says it was founded in 1982 and is known for its ad line "lobster bigger than a little girl". Its website also keeps clips of a TVB food show visit. Traceable shop history like this is more useful than unsourced celebrity stories.
en.hours: Lunch 11:00–14:30; dinner 17:00–22:30; usually closed Tuesdays (except public holidays and their eves)
en.price: Live seafood by type, weight and market price; other dishes per menu
en.access_notes: Booking recommended; say whether you want indoor or outdoor seating. WhatsApp +65 9830 5276; other phone +65 6778 7198. Don't budget as you would for a regular hawker stall.
en.review_summary: In 2025 reviews, some diners liked the pumpkin sauce crab, orh nee and service; others were disappointed with the crab meat and the standard of some dishes. Both positive and negative feedback are kept. Reviews are no substitute for confirming weight and price before ordering.

en.summary: From dinosaur fossils to the plants, animals and biodiversity of Southeast Asia. Good for anyone interested in nature, specimens and the history of science. It is also a stop for learning about Singapore's natural heritage, and pairs with the neighbouring NUS Museum for a half-day indoor route.
en.fun_fact: The three sauropod dinosaurs are named Prince, Apollonia and Twinky. In a 2025 research interview, the museum noted that Twinky's almost complete spine is rare. The fossils are not just for display; they are still used in classification research.
en.price: Official adult prices: S$18 for eligible residents, S$27 standard. Current NUS students and staff may enter free under the rules.
en.access_notes: Enquiries: nhmvisit@nus.edu.sg. The website says some exhibits in the mammal zone are being cleared, with the whole zone expected to close for renovation from late November. For tickets and eligibility, follow the official website. From Clementi, connect by bus.
en.review_summary: 2025 visitors found the collection rich and the volunteer guides helpful, but complained that buying tickets was a hassle. Earlier reviews liked the dinosaurs and local natural history. Check the official website for current ticketing.

en.summary: A free museum in the University Cultural Centre. It places Chinese art, Southeast Asian art and works by local sculptors in a research context. Take your time with the ceramics, calligraphy and paintings, and the current exhibitions. It also adds a university and regional-exchange angle to "Singapore culture".
en.fun_fact: Its origins go back to the University of Malaya Art Museum in 1955. Today its four collections hold more than 8,000 items, including works by Ng Eng Teng and the Peranakan collection of the Baba House.
en.hours: Tue–Sat 10:00–18:00; closed Sundays and public holidays; Mondays for booked school and staff visits only
en.price: Free for permanent and current public exhibitions; check sign-up details for specific events
en.access_notes: museum@nus.edu.sg. The website's visit page still shows an old 2024 notice about a temporary closure; this card does not take it to mean the museum is closed now. Groups of 20 or more must book.
en.review_summary: A 2023 visitor liked that it was free, air-conditioned and had Chinese art. A 2019 visitor said it had a strong research feel and a manageable size, and suggested allowing about 1.5 hours. These are a few personal experiences.

en.summary: A Peranakan family home museum on Neil Road, and an important place for understanding domestic space, household objects and identity. It is not on the NUS campus or in Clementi; it belongs to the Outram, Bukit Pasoh and Blair Plain neighbourhood route.
en.fun_fact: The house once belonged to descendants of shipping merchant Wee Bin's family. NUS acquired it through a donation, researched and restored it, and opened it in 2008, keeping the home as a place to understand Peranakan life.
en.hours: Closed for restoration from 2025-05-31 until 2027; no visits inside the house
en.price: No regular entry during the closure
en.access_notes: The museum has confirmed the restoration, so automatic routes exclude it. You can ask about Blair Plain neighbourhood tours and the online virtual exhibition. babahouse@nus.edu.sg.
en.review_summary: Visitors in 2023–2024, before the restoration, said the guided tours were in-depth and helped them understand Peranakan family life, and stressed that booking was required. It is closed now, so these past experiences don't mean you can go inside today.

en.summary: A one-of-a-kind cultural site that puts folk tales, moral ideas and exaggerated sculptures in one space. Visitors of different ages may react very differently. Scenes such as the Ten Courts of Hell can start conversations about moral stories, but check the exhibits first if you bring children.
en.fun_fact: The sculptures in the park date back to 1937. They turn written stories into scenes, showing how early Chinese society passed on values visually.
en.hours: Hell's Museum daily 10:00–18:00, last entry 17:00; check the outer park's hours separately
en.price: Hell's Museum is paid; follow the official ticketing page
en.access_notes: The outer park and the paid museum are separate. Don't climb the sculptures. Some displays are quite graphic, so families should read up first. enquiry@hellsmuseum.com.sg.
en.review_summary: 2026 visitors found the mythological sculptures unique but the outdoors hot and some facilities dated. In 2025, some liked the free park but felt the paid Hell's Museum was not good value. Different views are kept.

en.summary: An older neighbourhood hawker centre opposite West Coast Plaza, a place to look at duck rice, nasi lemak, handmade noodles and oyster omelette. Current searches show it is closed for renovation, so it stays in the collection and will be added to real routes after it reopens.
en.fun_fact: Chinese braised dishes, Malay breakfasts and handmade snacks sit side by side in one market. It suits a culture stop framed as "different families' breakfasts" rather than just rating the whole centre.
en.hours: Records show it closed for renovation 2026-09-14 to 12-27, expected to reopen 12-28; confirm with NEA / town council notices
en.price: Not recommended for meals during the renovation
en.access_notes: A recent food guide cites NEA closure dates, but visitor platforms still show it as open. This card takes the cautious approach: it is kept out of automatic routes, and the closure details are marked as secondary-source, pending official confirmation.
en.review_summary: 2025 visitors liked the affordable choices and neighbourhood feel. An August 2026 visitor reminded people to bring cash or a working local QR payment method. Both are from before the renovation and don't show that it is open now.

en.summary: On Level 5 of Clementi Mall, linked to the MRT station and bus interchange. A very everyday Singapore public cultural space. Good as a rainy-day option or a route start or end point, and a look at how community reading services fit inside a shopping mall.
en.fun_fact: NLB records that this library was first to launch the Mystery Brown Bag: themed books packed into a bag, so people passing by at lunch can discover something to read like opening a surprise bag.
en.hours: Daily 11:00–21:00; extended hours 09:00–11:00 without full staffed service; closed on public holidays
en.price: Free entry; borrowing follows membership rules
en.access_notes: Closes early at 17:00 on the eves of Christmas, New Year and Chinese New Year. Seats, power points and quietness are not guaranteed; go by what you find on site and NLB notices.
en.review_summary: A parent blogger liked the themed book picks, the children's reading corner and being close to the MRT. The article's date was not confirmed this round, so it can't guarantee current quietness or seating.

en.summary: Along Telok Ayer Street, see the seafaring faith of Hokkien migrants, clan association mutual aid and traditional architecture. Take your time with the front and rear halls, carved stone pillars and cut-porcelain roof ridges. Combine it with the mosque and the Indian Muslim shrine heritage centre on the same street for a multi-faith walk.
en.fun_fact: The temple once faced the shore, and newly arrived migrants would give thanks to Mazu here. The main hall keeps a plaque reading "Bo Jing Nan Ming" (calm waves over the southern seas), given by the Guangxu Emperor in 1907.
en.hours: Opening hours not verified day by day; check the temple's notices before visiting
en.price: Free; offerings and donations are voluntary
en.access_notes: A working temple; photography is not allowed in some shrine areas. Follow the signs on site.
en.coordinates_note: Checked against the place marker on public maps; not measured on site, and not guaranteed to mark an accessible entrance.
en.verification_note: 2026-10-29 is the date web sources were checked, not a site visit date. Re-check changeable details before you go.
en.review_summary: 2025 reviews said it was quiet with fine carvings, and the English explanations helped. Others noted it is small and good for a short stop. (These reviews are personal experiences from a small sample.)

en.summary: An old Teochew temple surrounded by financial district towers. Its two side-by-side halls are dedicated to Mazu and Xuan Tian Shang Di. The opera figures, colourful cut-porcelain and woodcarvings on the roof are more worth your time than a front-on photo. Visit it alongside the story of Teochew migrants and Ngee Ann Kongsi.
en.fun_fact: In 1899 the Guangxu Emperor granted the plaque "Shu Hai Xiang Yun" (auspicious clouds over the dawn sea), linked to the local community's relief for floods in Shandong. Its 2014 restoration won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award of Excellence for Cultural Heritage Conservation.
en.hours: Opening hours not verified day by day; check the temple's notices before visiting
en.access_notes: Respect on-site management and photography rules.
en.coordinates_note: Checked against the place marker on public maps; not measured on site, and not guaranteed to mark an accessible entrance.
en.verification_note: 2026-10-29 is the date web sources were checked, not a site visit date. Re-check changeable details before you go.
en.review_summary: An October 2025 visitor especially liked the porcelain figures on the roof, but felt the surrounding towers took away from the old temple's sense of space. A 2022 review found it small and quiet. (These reviews are personal experiences from a small sample.)
